A method for binaural synthesis of at least one virtual sound source comprises operating a first device comprising at least four physical sound sources, wherein, when the first device is used by a user, at least two physical sound sources are positioned closer to a first ear of the user than to a second ear, and at least two physical sound sources are positioned closer to the second ear than to the first ear, and wherein, for each ear, at least two physical sound sources are configured to acoustically induce natural directional pinna cues associated with different directions of sound arrival at the ear of the user. The method further comprises receiving and processing at least one audio input signal and distributing at least one processed version of the audio input signal at least between 4 kHz and 12 kHz over at least two physical sound sources for each ear.

outputs.L2: A technique for binaurally rendering one or more virtual sound sources involves using a first device that includes no fewer than four physical sound emitters. When the device is worn or otherwise used by a user, at least two of the emitters are located nearer to the user’s first ear than to the second ear, while at least two other emitters are located nearer to the second ear than to the first ear. For each ear, two or more of the physical sound emitters are arranged to produce natural pinna-related directional acoustic cues corresponding to different incoming sound directions at that ear. The technique also includes accepting at least one audio input signal, processing that signal, and delivering at least one processed form of it, within at least the 4 kHz to 12 kHz frequency range, across at least two physical sound emitters for each ear.
outputs.L3:
The method provides binaural synthesis for at least one virtual sound source by using a first device that includes at least four physical sound sources, such as loudspeakers or acoustic transducers. The physical sound sources are arranged relative to a listener’s head so that they can reproduce spatial audio cues associated with the virtual sound source.

At least two of the physical sound sources are positioned closer to one ear of the listener, while at least two other physical sound sources are positioned closer to the other ear. This arrangement allows each ear to be addressed by multiple nearby physical sound sources, rather than by a single source. As a result, the system can generate more convincing spatial effects and improve the perception of direction, distance, and externalization of the virtual sound source.

For each ear, at least two corresponding physical sound sources are configured to produce natural directional pinna cues from different sound arrival directions. In other words, the sound reaching each ear can be emitted from multiple physical directions, enabling the listener’s outer ear, or pinna, to shape the sound in a manner similar to how it would shape sound arriving from real-world directions. These pinna-related cues are particularly important for perceiving elevation, front-back position, and other spatial characteristics of a sound source.

The method further includes receiving at least one audio input signal associated with the virtual sound source and processing that audio input signal to generate binaural audio information. The processing may include filtering, equalization, spatial rendering, frequency-dependent distribution, or other signal-processing operations that support the creation of a desired perceived position of the virtual sound source.

In particular, the processed audio signal is distributed, within a frequency range from 4 kHz to 12 kHz, over at least two physical sound sources for each ear. By distributing this high-frequency portion of the signal among multiple sound sources near each ear, the method enhances the generation of natural pinna cues and improves the listener’s ability to localize the virtual sound source. Thus, the method enables binaural synthesis using a multi-source device configuration that supports more realistic spatial audio reproduction.
outputs.L4:
A binaural synthesis method is described in which a playback device includes at least four physical sound sources arranged in the vicinity of a listener’s ears. The sound sources may be positioned so that, for each ear, more than one source is available to radiate sound from different spatial positions relative to the outer ear. For example, the device may include two or more miniature loudspeakers near the left ear and two or more miniature loudspeakers near the right ear, with the sources placed at different vertical, horizontal, or angular locations around the pinna.

In operation, an audio input signal is received and processed to generate binaural output signals corresponding to a desired virtual sound source position. The processing may divide the signal into frequency bands, with particular emphasis on the high-frequency range between approximately 4 kHz and 12 kHz. This frequency range is important because it contains spectral cues created by the shape of the listener’s outer ear, or pinna. These cues vary depending on the direction from which sound arrives and help the listener distinguish whether a sound is in front, behind, above, below, or at another spatial location.

Instead of reproducing the high-frequency content for each ear from only a single sound source, the method distributes these components across multiple physical sound sources associated with that ear. By controlling the relative level, timing, phase, or filtering of the signals sent to the different sources, the system can cause the sound to interact with the pinna in a manner similar to sound arriving naturally from a particular direction. In this way, the device acoustically induces ear-specific directional cues rather than relying solely on conventional electronic filtering.

The lower-frequency components of the audio signal may be reproduced using one or more of the same sound sources, or they may be processed separately, since low-frequency spatial perception is generally less dependent on fine pinna-related spectral effects. The high-frequency components, however, are selectively routed and weighted among the multiple sources near each ear so that the resulting acoustic field at the ear more closely matches the cues associated with the intended virtual source location.

As a result, the method enables virtual sound sources to be rendered with improved naturalness and spatial accuracy. A listener may perceive sounds as originating from positions outside the head and from more precise directions than would be possible with ordinary headphone reproduction. By physically presenting high-frequency sound from different positions around each ear, the system can recreate directional pinna cues that support a more convincing binaural listening experience for music, communication, gaming, augmented reality, virtual reality, and other spatial-audio applications.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” may be one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, but it plays an important role in communication. As a definite article, “the” helps us refer to something specific or already known. For example, saying “a book” could mean any book, but saying “the book” points to a particular one.

This simple word adds clarity and precision to sentences. It helps readers and listeners understand exactly what is being discussed. Whether we are talking about “the sun,” “the city,” or “the answer,” the word “the” guides attention toward something defined and recognizable.

Although it is easy to overlook, “the” is essential in everyday language. It connects ideas, gives meaning to nouns, and makes communication smoother. In many ways, “the” proves that even the smallest words can have a big impact.
